content: Adults and older adults with chronic conditions should engage in regular physical activity. It is strongly recommended, based on moderate-certainty evidence, that they perform at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or at least 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of moderateand vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week to achieve substantial health benefits. Additionally, adults and older adults with chronic conditions should incorporate muscle-strengthening activities of moderate or greater intensity that target all major muscle groups on two or more days per week, as these provide additional health benefits. This recommendation is also strongly supported by moderate-certainty evidence. For older adults with chronic conditions, it is further recommended that their weekly physical activity include varied, multicomponent exercises emphasizing functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on three or more days per week. This approach aims to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. This recommendation is strongly supported by moderate-certainty evidence. When not contraindicated, adults and older adults with chronic conditions may increase their moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity to more than 300 minutes per week, or perform more than 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of moderateand vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week for additional health benefits. This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. If individuals with chronic conditions are unable to meet the above recommendations, they should aim to engage in physical activity according to their abilities. They are encouraged to start with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration over time. Consulting with a physical activity specialist or healthcare professional is advised to tailor the type and amount of activity to their individual needs, abilities, functional limitations, complications, medications, and overall treatment plan. Physical activity has been shown to promote beneficial shortand long-term changes in metabolic, hormonal, and inflammatory pathways, which are thought to be protective against cancer incidence and improve survival outcomes. Greater amounts of physical activity after a cancer diagnosis are associated with lower risks of all-cause, cancer-specific, and cause-specific mortality in survivors of breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether physical activity reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or second primary cancers. For individuals with hypertension, physical activity is associated with reduced cardiovascular disease mortality, improved physical function, better health-related quality of life, and slower disease progression (as measured by blood pressure response to exercise). Emerging evidence suggests that physically active individuals with hypertension experience significantly better health-related quality of life compared to their inactive counterparts. In adults with type 2 diabetes, physical activity, including aerobic and muscle-strengthening exercises, is associated with improved secondary markers of disease progression, such as HbA1c, blood pressure, BMI, and lipid profiles. Resistance training, particularly high-intensity resistance training, has been shown to significantly reduce HbA1c levels and improve fasting insulin levels. However, there is insufficient evidence to assess the effects of physical activity on health-related quality of life and physical function in this population. For people living with HIV, physical activity improves cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and health-related quality of life. It also reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety. Interventions involving aerobic exercise or a combination of aerobic and progressive muscle-strengthening exercises, performed for at least 30 minutes three times per week, have demonstrated these benefits. Importantly, physical activity does not adversely affect markers of HIV disease progression, such as CD4 count or viral load, indicating that HIV as a chronic condition is not negatively impacted by regular exercise. The evidence supports a dose-response relationship between physical activity and health outcomes. For cancer survivors, greater amounts of physical activity after diagnosis are linked to lower risks of all-cause and cancer-specific mortality. For individuals with hypertension, higher levels of physical activity attenuate the increased risk of cardiovascular disease mortality associated with elevated systolic blood pressure. Similarly, in adults with type 2 diabetes, higher volumes of physical activity are associated with progressively reduced cardiovascular mortality risk. Most interventions for these populations are based on 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity per week, along with 2–3 sessions of resistance training. While evidence supports the benefits of aerobic and resistance activities, further research is needed to explore the effects of specific types of physical activity, such as Tai Chi, yoga, or Qigong, and to establish more precise dose-response relationships for mental health and quality of life outcomes. Overall, the benefits of regular physical activity for cancer survivors and individuals with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and HIV outweigh the risks. Engaging in physical activity consistent with the recommended guidelines provides favorable health outcomes, including improved disease markers, reduced mortality risks, and enhanced quality of life.
